question: A 68-year-old man with progressive exertional breathlessness and bilateral lower extremity swelling is found to have a harsh systolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border that peaks mid-systole. Which valvular lesion most likely explains his presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Calcific narrowing of the aortic outflow valve causing obstructed ejection
options.rationale: Aortic valve narrowing produces a crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the right second intercostal space and increases LV systolic pressure with reduced stroke volume, explaining dyspnea and peripheral edema via progressive LV dysfunction.

options.text: Incomplete closure of the aortic valve causing diastolic backflow into the ventricle
options.rationale: Aortic insufficiency causes a diastolic murmur and widened pulse pressure with increased LVEDV; it would present with a diastolic rather than a systolic ejection murmur, so this finding would be correct only if the murmur occurred in diastole.

options.text: Narrowing of the mitral inflow orifice limiting ventricular filling
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis raises LA pressure and causes a diastolic murmur and reduced LVEDV; it does not produce a right upper sternal border systolic ejection murmur, so it would be correct only if auscultation localized to the apex with a diastolic rumble.

options.text: Failure of the mitral leaflets to coapt producing systolic backflow into the atrium
options.rationale: Mitral regurgitation causes a holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex and elevated LA v waves; it would be correct only if the murmur were apical and pansystolic rather than a right-sided ejection murmur.

options.text: Primary myocardial pump failure without a discrete valvular lesion
options.rationale: Systolic heart failure can cause pulmonary congestion and edema but typically lacks a localized crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border; this would be correct only if no valvular murmur were present.

question: Which change in left ventricular hemodynamics is expected immediately after the onset of severe obstruction to outflow at the aortic valve?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume, and associated electrical events and heart sounds that occur during a normal cardiac cycle.

options.text: Marked rise in peak left ventricular systolic pressure relative to aortic pressure
options.rationale: Obstruction increases afterload so LV systolic pressure must rise to generate flow across the stenotic valve, producing a large LV–aortic pressure gradient as described for aortic stenosis.

options.text: Immediate large increase in left ventricular end diastolic volume
options.rationale: LVEDV increases chronically with regurgitant lesions; acute outflow obstruction raises LVESV and may reduce stroke volume but does not immediately cause a large LVEDV increase unless chronic remodeling occurs.

options.text: Decrease in left atrial pressure due to reduced forward flow
options.rationale: Reduced forward flow tends to increase upstream pressures; LA pressure would not fall and would rise if LV filling is impaired, so this option would be correct only if systemic venous return fell dramatically.

options.text: Lowered aortic systolic pressure with preserved aortic diastolic pressure
options.rationale: Severe obstruction often lowers aortic systolic pressure and may not preserve diastolic pressure; this would be correct only if compensatory mechanisms maintained diastolic pressure despite reduced systolic ejection.

options.text: Immediate appearance of a diastolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: Aortic outflow obstruction produces a systolic ejection murmur; a new diastolic apical murmur would indicate a different lesion such as mitral stenosis or aortic regurgitation and would be correct only in that context.

question: A patient with chronic aortic valve narrowing develops concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Which heart sound is most likely to be accentuated by the resulting ventricular stiffness?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: A low frequency sound occurring just before the first heart sound
options.rationale: An S4 (atrial gallop) occurs in late diastole just before S1 and is caused by atrial contraction into a stiff hypertrophied ventricle, which is typical in pressure overload such as aortic stenosis.

options.text: A high frequency sound occurring at the onset of ventricular systole
options.rationale: S1 is high-pitched and marks AV valve closure at systole onset; it is not specifically accentuated by ventricular stiffness and would be correct only if mitral valve closure dynamics changed.

options.text: A low frequency sound occurring shortly after the second heart sound
options.rationale: S3 occurs early in diastole after S2 and is associated with rapid filling and dilated ventricles; it would be correct only in volume overload states rather than concentric hypertrophy.

options.text: A split second heart sound that widens with inspiration
options.rationale: Physiologic S2 splitting varies with respiration and relates to A2/P2 timing; it is not a marker of ventricular stiffness and would be correct only if pulmonary valve closure were delayed.

options.text: A high frequency sound heard during mid-diastole at the apex
options.rationale: Mid-diastolic sounds at the apex suggest a rumbling diastolic murmur (e.g., mitral stenosis) rather than a discrete heart sound caused by ventricular stiffness; this would be correct only with mitral inflow obstruction.

question: Which atrial pressure waveform component corresponds to atrial contraction and contributes to a late increase in ventricular filling?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: The a wave representing atrial systole
options.rationale: The 'a' wave on atrial pressure tracing is produced by atrial contraction (atrial systole) and corresponds to the atrial kick that augments late ventricular filling.

options.text: The c wave representing ventricular contraction bulging the valve
options.rationale: The 'c' wave reflects bulging of the AV valve into the atrium during isovolumic ventricular contraction, not active atrial contraction; it would be correct only if the question asked about valve bulging.

options.text: The v wave representing peak atrial pressure from venous return
options.rationale: The 'v' wave is due to venous filling of the atrium during ventricular systole and peaks before AV valve opening; it is not the atrial contraction wave and would be correct only if asking about passive atrial filling.

options.text: The y descent representing rapid atrial emptying
options.rationale: The 'y' descent follows the v wave and reflects atrial emptying when the AV valve opens; it is not the contraction wave and would be correct only if the lead-in asked about valve opening dynamics.

options.text: A sustained plateau during ventricular ejection
options.rationale: A sustained plateau is not a named atrial waveform component; this would be correct only if the tracing lacked discrete a, c, v waves and showed continuous pressure elevation.

question: A patient with chronic aortic regurgitation is expected to have which pattern of aortic pressures?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Elevated systolic pressure with reduced diastolic pressure producing wide pulse pressure
options.rationale: Aortic regurgitation causes diastolic runoff into the LV lowering diastolic aortic pressure while increased stroke volume raises systolic pressure, producing an increased pulse pressure as described in the lecture.

options.text: Reduced systolic pressure with preserved diastolic pressure producing narrow pulse pressure
options.rationale: Narrow pulse pressure is seen with low stroke volume states; this would be correct only if forward output were severely reduced without diastolic runoff, not in AR.

options.text: Uniformly elevated aortic pressure throughout the cardiac cycle
options.rationale: Uniform elevation suggests systemic hypertension affecting both systole and diastole; AR specifically lowers diastolic pressure, so this would be correct only with concomitant severe hypertension preventing diastolic fall.

options.text: Markedly reduced diastolic pressure with unchanged systolic pressure
options.rationale: AR typically increases systolic pressure via increased stroke volume; unchanged systolic pressure would be correct only if compensatory mechanisms failed to augment systolic output.

options.text: Aortic pressure tracing with early diastolic notch and normal pulse pressure
options.rationale: An early diastolic notch is not characteristic of AR and normal pulse pressure contradicts the expected widened pulse pressure; this would be correct only if AR were absent.

question: Which murmur timing and location best match a regurgitant lesion of the mitral valve?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: Holosystolic murmur loudest at the cardiac apex
options.rationale: Mitral regurgitation produces a pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur best heard at the apex due to systolic backflow from LV to LA, consistent with the lecture description.

options.text: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border
options.rationale: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border is typical of aortic regurgitation, not mitral regurgitation; it would be correct only if the lesion were aortic.

options.text: Mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap at the apex
options.rationale: A mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap is characteristic of mitral stenosis; this would be correct only if the mitral orifice were narrowed rather than regurgitant.

options.text: Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border
options.rationale: A systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border indicates aortic stenosis; it would be correct only for an aortic outflow lesion, not mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Continuous machinery murmur heard throughout systole and diastole
options.rationale: A continuous machinery murmur suggests a patent ductus arteriosus and is unrelated to mitral valve pathology; it would be correct only if a PDA were present.

question: During the isovolumic contraction phase, which event is responsible for the first heart sound?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: Closure of the atrioventricular valves at ventricular systole onset
options.rationale: S1 is generated by mitral (and tricuspid) valve closure during isovolumic contraction as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, as stated in the lecture.

options.text: Closure of the semilunar valves at the end of ejection
options.rationale: Semilunar valve closure produces S2 during isovolumic relaxation, not S1; this option would be correct only if referring to the second heart sound.

options.text: Rapid filling of the ventricle after mitral opening
options.rationale: Rapid ventricular filling occurs in early diastole and can produce S3 in dilated ventricles; it is not the cause of S1 and would be correct only in volume overload contexts.

options.text: Atrial contraction producing the atrial kick
options.rationale: Atrial contraction corresponds to the 'a' wave and contributes to late diastolic filling; it does not generate S1 and would be correct only if the question asked about atrial sounds.

options.text: Bulging of the semilunar valves into the ventricle during ejection
options.rationale: Bulging of semilunar valves is not the mechanism for S1; valve bulging into the atrium (AV valve bulge) produces the 'c' wave on atrial tracing and would be correct only for that waveform.

question: A patient with long-standing mitral stenosis is most likely to develop which downstream hemodynamic consequence?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Elevated left atrial pressure with pulmonary venous congestion
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis impedes LV filling, raising LA pressure which transmits to pulmonary veins causing congestion and symptoms like dyspnea, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Marked increase in left ventricular end systolic volume
options.rationale: MS reduces LVEDV and stroke volume rather than primarily increasing LVESV; LVESV would rise mainly with systolic dysfunction or outflow obstruction, not isolated MS.

options.text: Widened aortic pulse pressure with bounding pulses
options.rationale: Widened pulse pressure is characteristic of aortic regurgitation due to increased stroke volume and low diastolic pressure; it would be correct only in AR.

options.text: Holosystolic murmur loudest at the right upper sternal border
options.rationale: A holosystolic murmur at the right upper sternal border is not typical of MS; MS produces a diastolic rumble at the apex, so this would be correct only with a different lesion.

options.text: Prominent third heart sound from rapid ventricular filling
options.rationale: S3 is associated with volume overload and dilated ventricles; MS causes reduced LV filling and would not typically produce an S3 unless secondary volume overload developed.

question: Which waveform change on the atrial pressure tracing is most prominent in severe mitral regurgitation?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: A tall v wave reflecting systolic backflow into the atrium
options.rationale: Mitral regurgitation causes systolic flow from LV to LA producing a large 'v' wave on atrial pressure tracing, as emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: A large a wave reflecting exaggerated atrial contraction
options.rationale: A large 'a' wave occurs with increased resistance to atrial emptying (e.g., AV block or stiff ventricle); MR produces a tall 'v' wave rather than an isolated large 'a' wave.

options.text: A prominent c wave due to valve prolapse into the atrium
options.rationale: The 'c' wave is due to ventricular contraction bulging the AV valve; while valve prolapse can alter waveforms, the diagnostic MR feature is the tall 'v' wave, so this would be correct only with specific valve anatomy.

options.text: Flattening of all atrial waveform components
options.rationale: Flattening would suggest low atrial pressures or poor tracing quality; MR increases atrial pressures and produces a tall v wave, so flattening would be correct only with measurement artifact.

options.text: An early y descent with delayed mitral opening
options.rationale: An early y descent is seen when the AV valve opens and atrial emptying occurs; MR typically elevates v waves and may alter y descent but the hallmark is the tall v wave, so this would be correct only in a different hemodynamic pattern.

question: A 55-year-old with chronic volume overload from valvular disease develops an audible low-pitched sound shortly after S2. Which structural change most likely produced this sound?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Rapid filling of a dilated ventricle producing a third heart sound
options.rationale: S3 occurs early in diastole after S2 when rapid filling into an enlarged, compliant ventricle produces low-frequency vibrations; the lecture links S3 to dilated ventricles and volume overload.

options.text: Atrial contraction into a stiff hypertrophied ventricle producing a fourth sound
options.rationale: S4 occurs before S1 with atrial kick into a stiff ventricle; it is late diastolic and would not occur shortly after S2, so this would be correct only if the timing were late diastole.

options.text: Closure of the semilunar valves producing the second heart sound
options.rationale: S2 is high-pitched and occurs at the onset of isovolumic relaxation; it is not a low-pitched sound after S2 and would be correct only if the described sound were S2 itself.

options.text: Opening snap of a stenotic atrioventricular valve in early systole
options.rationale: An opening snap occurs in early diastole with mitral stenosis and is not a low-pitched S3 after S2; this would be correct only if the sound were an opening snap rather than S3.

options.text: A continuous machinery murmur from a persistent arterial connection
options.rationale: A continuous machinery murmur (e.g., PDA) is audible throughout systole and diastole and is not a discrete low-pitched sound after S2; it would be correct only with a PDA present.

question: Which of the following best explains why patients with aortic stenosis may develop exertional syncope?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Fixed outflow obstruction limits cardiac output increase during exertion
options.rationale: Severe aortic valve narrowing prevents adequate rise in stroke volume during activity, causing hypotension and cerebral hypoperfusion; the lecture notes reduced SV and high LV pressure in AS leading to exertional symptoms.

options.text: Diastolic backflow into the ventricle reduces forward stroke volume
options.rationale: Diastolic backflow describes aortic regurgitation, which widens pulse pressure and increases LVEDV; it would cause different symptoms and would be correct only if AR were the lesion.

options.text: Elevated left atrial pressure causes reflex bradycardia and syncope
options.rationale: Elevated LA pressure leads to pulmonary congestion and dyspnea rather than reflex bradycardia causing syncope; this would be correct only if an abnormal reflex mediated sudden bradycardia were documented.

options.text: Peripheral vasodilation during exertion causes acute mitral valve prolapse
options.rationale: Peripheral vasodilation does not acutely produce mitral valve prolapse; syncope from AS is due to fixed obstruction, so this distractor would be correct only with a different pathophysiology.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism from venous stasis leads to sudden right heart failure
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism can cause syncope but is unrelated to chronic aortic valve narrowing; this would be correct only if there were evidence of acute thromboembolism.

question: A patient with suspected aortic regurgitation has a bounding carotid pulse and wide pulse pressure on exam. Which ventricular volume change underlies these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume, and associated electrical events and heart sounds that occur during a normal cardiac cycle.

options.text: Chronic increase in left ventricular end diastolic volume from diastolic backflow
options.rationale: AR causes diastolic regurgitation into the LV increasing LVEDV; increased stroke volume produces bounding pulses and widened pulse pressure, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Acute decrease in left ventricular end systolic volume from improved ejection
options.rationale: A decrease in LVESV would raise stroke volume but is not the primary mechanism in AR; the hallmark is increased LVEDV from regurgitation, so this would be correct only with isolated enhanced contractility.

options.text: Reduced left ventricular preload due to impaired venous return
options.rationale: Reduced preload lowers stroke volume and pulse pressure; this contradicts bounding pulses and would be correct only if venous return were diminished.

options.text: Marked increase in left atrial volume causing transmitted pulses
options.rationale: LA enlargement affects pulmonary pressures and symptoms but does not directly cause bounding carotid pulses; this would be correct only if LA dynamics somehow altered systemic pulse contour.

options.text: Fixed low stroke volume with narrow pulse pressure
options.rationale: Fixed low stroke volume produces narrow pulse pressure and weak pulses, opposite to the described findings; it would be correct only in severe outflow obstruction without compensatory volume changes.

question: Which auscultatory finding would you expect in a patient with left ventricular dilation from chronic mitral regurgitation?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: A holosystolic murmur at the apex often accompanied by an S3
options.rationale: Chronic MR produces a pansystolic murmur at the apex and volume overload can lead to ventricular dilation with an audible S3 during rapid filling, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: A high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border
options.rationale: An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border suggests aortic regurgitation, not MR; it would be correct only if AR were present instead of MR.

options.text: A mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex
options.rationale: A mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap is characteristic of mitral stenosis, not regurgitation; it would be correct only with MS.

options.text: A crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border
options.rationale: That pattern is typical of aortic stenosis and would be correct only if the lesion were at the aortic valve rather than the mitral valve.

options.text: A continuous machinery murmur heard best below the left clavicle
options.rationale: A continuous machinery murmur indicates a PDA and is unrelated to MR; it would be correct only if a PDA were the actual lesion.

question: Which phase of the cardiac cycle immediately follows the QRS complex on the ECG and is characterized by rising ventricular pressure with closed valves?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: Isovolumic contraction phase with both AV and semilunar valves closed
options.rationale: After the QRS (ventricular depolarization) the ventricles contract in a closed chamber raising pressure without volume change; this is the isovolumic contraction phase described in the lecture.

options.text: Rapid ventricular filling phase with open AV valves
options.rationale: Rapid filling occurs after mitral opening in diastole and follows ventricular relaxation, not the QRS; this would be correct only if the timing were diastolic.

options.text: Isovolumic relaxation phase with semilunar valves closed
options.rationale: Isovolumic relaxation follows aortic valve closure after ejection and corresponds to ventricular repolarization (T wave), not the QRS; it would be correct only with different ECG timing.

options.text: Atrial systole producing the atrial kick before ventricular contraction
options.rationale: Atrial systole corresponds to the P wave and occurs before the QRS; it would be correct only if the question asked about events preceding the QRS.

options.text: Reduced ejection phase with declining ventricular pressure
options.rationale: Reduced ejection occurs later in systole after peak pressure and during ejection, not immediately after the QRS; this would be correct only if ejection began immediately at depolarization without isovolumic contraction.

question: A patient with rheumatic mitral valve disease has an enlarged left atrium and low stroke volume. Which murmur timing best matches this lesion?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: A diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap at the apex
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis produces a diastolic rumble and an opening snap due to a stiff, narrowed mitral valve and elevated LA pressure with reduced LVEDV, matching the lecture description.

options.text: A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
options.rationale: A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border suggests tricuspid regurgitation or MR at the apex; it would be correct only if the regurgitant lesion were present.

options.text: A high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the right upper sternal border
options.rationale: An early diastolic murmur at the right upper sternal border indicates aortic regurgitation, not mitral stenosis; it would be correct only with AR.

options.text: A crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: A crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the apex is not typical; aortic stenosis produces that pattern at the right upper sternal border, so this would be correct only with atypical auscultation.

options.text: A continuous murmur heard best in the interscapular area
options.rationale: A continuous murmur in the interscapular area is not characteristic of mitral stenosis and would be correct only with unusual vascular anomalies.

question: Which of the following best describes the ventricular volume change labeled as stroke volume on the pressure-volume loop?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: The difference between end diastolic and end systolic ventricular volumes
options.rationale: Stroke volume equals EDV minus ESV (volume ejected during systole), which is the width of the PV loop base as defined in the lecture.

options.text: The total ventricular volume at end systole
options.rationale: End systolic volume is the residual volume after ejection and is not the stroke volume; this would be correct only if stroke volume were defined incorrectly.

options.text: The ventricular volume at the onset of isovolumic contraction
options.rationale: Volume at onset of isovolumic contraction equals EDV but stroke volume is the change from EDV to ESV; this would be correct only if no ejection occurred.

options.text: The sum of atrial and ventricular volumes at end diastole
options.rationale: Stroke volume is not a sum of chamber volumes; this would be correct only in a nonphysiologic measurement combining chambers.

options.text: The difference between aortic and ventricular pressures during ejection
options.rationale: Pressure difference influences flow but stroke volume is a volume change, not a pressure difference; this would be correct only if stroke volume were measured indirectly from pressure gradients.

question: A patient with left bundle branch block has paradoxical splitting of S2. Which mechanism from the lecture explains this finding?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Delayed left ventricular contraction prolongs aortic valve closure
options.rationale: Paradoxical splitting occurs when A2 is delayed relative to P2, as in LBBB or prolonged LV ejection (e.g., AS), causing the split to be more evident in expiration, matching the lecture.

options.text: Delayed right ventricular contraction prolongs pulmonary valve closure
options.rationale: Delayed RV contraction causes wide splitting (P2 delayed), seen in RBBB or pulmonic stenosis; paradoxical splitting specifically involves delayed A2, so this would be correct only in RBBB.

options.text: Fixed interatrial communication causing constant splitting
options.rationale: Fixed splitting is due to ASD causing constant A2-P2 separation independent of respiration; paradoxical splitting is different and would be correct only with an ASD.

options.text: Early closure of the aortic valve before pulmonary closure
options.rationale: Early aortic closure would produce normal or reversed timing but paradoxical splitting requires delayed aortic closure; this would be correct only if A2 occurred earlier than P2.

options.text: Increased pulmonary arterial capacitance delaying pulmonary valve closure
options.rationale: Increased PA capacitance delays P2 and causes wide splitting, not paradoxical splitting; this would be correct only in volume overload lesions affecting the right heart.

question: Which clinical sign from the lecture is most directly explained by elevated pulmonary venous pressure secondary to left atrial hypertension?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Bilateral crackles at the lung bases from pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Elevated LA pressure transmits to pulmonary veins and capillaries causing pulmonary congestion and crackles, as noted for MS and MR in the lecture.

options.text: Bounding peripheral pulses from widened pulse pressure
options.rationale: Bounding pulses result from widened pulse pressure in AR due to increased stroke volume and low diastolic pressure; this is not caused by elevated pulmonary venous pressure.

options.text: JVD from isolated left atrial hypertension
options.rationale: Jugular venous distension reflects right heart or systemic venous hypertension; LA hypertension causes pulmonary, not systemic venous, congestion and would be correct only with right heart involvement.

options.text: Apex displacement from pericardial effusion
options.rationale: Apex displacement is seen with cardiomegaly or pericardial effusion and is unrelated to pulmonary venous pressure; it would be correct only with structural enlargement.

options.text: A loud S1 from increased mitral valve mobility
options.rationale: A loud S1 is due to abrupt mitral closure and increased leaflet mobility; pulmonary venous congestion does not directly cause a loud S1 and this would be correct only with specific valve dynamics.

question: A 72-year-old with calcific aortic valve disease has reduced stroke volume and concentric LV hypertrophy. Which change in the pressure-volume loop best represents his condition?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: Upward shift of end systolic pressure with decreased loop width
options.rationale: Increased afterload raises LV systolic pressure (upward shift) and reduced stroke volume narrows the PV loop width; this matches the lecture description for aortic stenosis.

options.text: Rightward shift of end diastolic volume with increased loop width
options.rationale: Rightward shift and increased width indicate volume overload (e.g., AR or MR) with increased EDV and SV; this would be correct only in chronic regurgitation, not AS.

options.text: Downward shift of systolic pressure with increased loop width
options.rationale: A downward systolic shift with increased width suggests reduced afterload with increased stroke volume, opposite to AS; it would be correct only with vasodilation or AR compensation.

options.text: Narrow loop with decreased end systolic pressure and increased contractility
options.rationale: Decreased ESV and increased contractility widen stroke volume; a narrow loop with low ESP is inconsistent and would be correct only with measurement error.

options.text: Leftward shift with increased end systolic volume and increased compliance
options.rationale: Leftward shift with increased ESV and compliance is contradictory; increased ESV usually shifts rightward, so this would be correct only with atypical definitions.

question: Which auscultatory change is characteristic of physiologic splitting of the second heart sound during inspiration?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Widening of the A2-P2 interval with inspiration and fusion on expiration
options.rationale: Physiologic splitting occurs because inspiration delays P2 relative to A2, widening the split during inspiration and often fusing during expiration, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Paradoxical reversal where P2 precedes A2 during inspiration
options.rationale: Paradoxical splitting involves delayed A2 (e.g., LBBB or AS) so A2 follows P2; this is not physiologic splitting and would be correct only with delayed LV events.

options.text: Fixed splitting that does not vary with respiration
options.rationale: Fixed splitting is seen with ASD and does not change with respiration; physiologic splitting varies with inspiration, so this would be correct only with an interatrial shunt.

options.text: A single unsplit S2 during both inspiration and expiration
options.rationale: A single S2 occurs when A2 and P2 are fused; physiologic splitting produces a split on inspiration, so this would be correct only if splitting were absent.

options.text: A louder P2 component with no change in timing
options.rationale: Louder P2 without timing change does not describe physiologic splitting; it would be correct only if pulmonary pressures increased without conduction or timing effects.

question: A patient with chronic mitral regurgitation develops pulmonary edema. Which sequence best explains this progression?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Systolic backflow to left atrium increases LA pressure then raises pulmonary venous pressure
options.rationale: MR causes systolic regurgitation into the LA producing tall v waves and elevated LA pressure that transmits to pulmonary veins causing congestion and edema, as outlined in the lecture.

options.text: Diastolic aortic runoff lowers diastolic pressure causing pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Diastolic aortic runoff (AR) affects systemic pressures and LV volumes but does not directly raise pulmonary venous pressure; this would be correct only if AR coexisted with MR.

options.text: Impaired LV systolic ejection alone increases pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.rationale: Isolated LV systolic failure can raise pulmonary pressures, but MR specifically elevates LA pressure via regurgitation; this option would be correct only if systolic failure were the primary cause.

options.text: Mitral valve narrowing reduces LV filling causing pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis raises LA pressure and can cause pulmonary edema, but the mechanism is valve narrowing rather than systolic regurgitation; this would be correct only with MS.

options.text: Right heart failure causes backward transmission to pulmonary veins
options.rationale: Right heart failure raises systemic venous pressures and JVD rather than pulmonary venous pressure; pulmonary edema from right failure alone is uncommon and this would be correct only with combined pathology.

question: Which finding on the Wiggers diagram corresponds to the moment the aortic valve closes?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: Onset of isovolumic relaxation and the second heart sound
options.rationale: Aortic valve closure marks the start of isovolumic relaxation and generates S2, as described in the lecture where S2 occurs during isovolumic relaxation.

options.text: Beginning of isovolumic contraction and the first heart sound
options.rationale: Isovolumic contraction and S1 occur at mitral valve closure before aortic opening, not at aortic valve closure; this would be correct only if the question asked about S1 timing.

options.text: Opening of the mitral valve and rapid ventricular filling
options.rationale: Mitral opening begins ventricular filling in diastole and follows aortic valve closure; it is not simultaneous with aortic closure and would be correct only if timing were misassigned.

options.text: Peak ventricular pressure during ejection
options.rationale: Peak ventricular pressure occurs during ejection before aortic closure; aortic valve closure follows the ejection phase and would be correct only if ejection ended earlier.

options.text: The atrial 'a' wave produced by atrial contraction
options.rationale: The 'a' wave is generated by atrial contraction in late diastole and is unrelated to aortic valve closure; it would be correct only if the tracing were misinterpreted.

question: Which hemodynamic change is most characteristic of chronic aortic regurgitation rather than acute regurgitation, per the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Left ventricular dilation with increased end diastolic volume and stroke volume
options.rationale: Chronic AR leads to LV volume overload, remodeling and dilation with increased LVEDV and compensatory increased SV (Frank-Starling), as described in the lecture.

options.text: Sudden severe hypotension with small, weak pulses
options.rationale: Acute AR can cause abrupt hypotension and low pulses due to lack of time for compensation; this would be correct only in acute rather than chronic AR.

options.text: Marked reduction in left atrial pressure with pulmonary clearance
options.rationale: AR primarily affects LV volumes and aortic pressures; LA pressure reduction is not characteristic and would be correct only with unrelated hemodynamic changes.

options.text: Fixed narrow pulse pressure with low systolic pressure
options.rationale: Narrow pulse pressure is not typical of chronic AR, which widens pulse pressure; this would be correct only in low output states without regurgitation.

options.text: Immediate rise in pulmonary arterial pressure without LV remodeling
options.rationale: Pulmonary pressures may rise secondary to LV failure but chronic AR primarily causes LV dilation first; this would be correct only with advanced decompensation.

question: A patient with severe aortic stenosis has a delayed A2 component causing paradoxical S2 splitting. Which conduction abnormality from the lecture most commonly produces a similar finding?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Left bundle branch block delaying left ventricular activation
options.rationale: LBBB delays LV contraction and aortic valve closure (A2), producing paradoxical splitting where A2 follows P2, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Right bundle branch block delaying right ventricular activation
options.rationale: RBBB delays P2 and causes wide splitting, not paradoxical splitting; it would be correct only if P2 delay were the mechanism sought.

options.text: First degree AV block prolonging PR interval
options.rationale: First-degree AV block affects atrioventricular timing but does not delay aortic valve closure relative to pulmonary closure and would be correct only if atrial timing altered valve events.

options.text: Complete heart block causing independent atrial and ventricular rates
options.rationale: Complete heart block causes AV dissociation and variable splitting but paradoxical splitting is specifically linked to delayed LV ejection such as LBBB; this would be correct only with specific timing effects.

options.text: Sinus bradycardia prolonging the cardiac cycle uniformly
options.rationale: Sinus bradycardia lengthens intervals but does not selectively delay A2 relative to P2; paradoxical splitting requires delayed LV events and would be correct only with conduction delay.

question: Which physical exam finding from the lecture most directly indicates increased left ventricular end systolic volume in aortic stenosis?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: A soft or diminished carotid upstroke with a systolic ejection murmur
options.rationale: In AS reduced stroke volume and prolonged ejection produce a weak carotid upstroke despite a systolic ejection murmur; increased LVESV reduces forward pulse, matching lecture physiology.

options.text: Bounding peripheral pulses with wide pulse pressure
options.rationale: Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure are features of AR due to increased SV and low diastolic pressure, not increased LVESV in AS; this would be correct only in AR.

options.text: Loud S1 with a mid-diastolic rumble
options.rationale: Loud S1 and mid-diastolic rumble suggest mitral stenosis dynamics, not LVESV increase from AS; this would be correct only with MS.

options.text: A continuous machinery murmur over the back
options.rationale: A continuous murmur (e.g., PDA) is unrelated to LVESV in AS and would be correct only with a PDA present.

options.text: A loud S2 with wide physiologic splitting
options.rationale: A loud S2 with physiologic splitting is normal and not indicative of increased LVESV; paradoxical or pathologic splitting relates to conduction or valve disease, so this would be correct only in different contexts.

question: Which statement best summarizes the genesis of the 'c' wave on the atrial pressure tracing?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: Bulging of the atrioventricular valve into the atrium during ventricular contraction
options.rationale: The 'c' wave arises from ventricular contraction causing the AV valve to bulge toward the atrium, transiently raising atrial pressure, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Atrial contraction producing the atrial kick
options.rationale: Atrial contraction produces the 'a' wave, not the 'c' wave; this would be correct only if the waveform labels were swapped.

options.text: Venous return filling the atrium during ventricular systole
options.rationale: Venous return contributes to the 'v' wave during ventricular systole, not the 'c' wave; this would be correct only if the tracing timing were misinterpreted.

options.text: Closure of the semilunar valves at the end of systole
options.rationale: Semilunar valve closure produces S2 and is associated with isovolumic relaxation, not the 'c' wave; this would be correct only if atrial pressure changes were secondary to semilunar events.

options.text: Rapid atrial emptying into the ventricle when the AV valve opens
options.rationale: Rapid atrial emptying corresponds to the 'y' descent after the v wave and AV valve opening, not the 'c' wave; this would be correct only if the question asked about the y descent.

question: A patient with severe aortic stenosis is being evaluated for the cause of exertional dyspnea. Which sequence best links valve pathology to reduced exercise tolerance?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Increased LV afterload reduces stroke volume limiting cardiac output rise with exertion
options.rationale: AS increases afterload so the LV cannot augment stroke volume during activity, causing exertional dyspnea and syncope due to inadequate cardiac output, consistent with lecture pathophysiology.

options.text: Diastolic regurgitation increases LVEDV causing pulmonary congestion during exercise
options.rationale: Diastolic regurgitation (AR) increases LVEDV and can cause congestion, but the mechanism differs from AS; this would be correct only if AR were the primary lesion.

options.text: Mitral inflow obstruction reduces LV preload improving exercise tolerance
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis reduces LV preload and stroke volume, worsening exercise tolerance rather than improving it; this would be correct only with paradoxical hemodynamics.

options.text: Right ventricular failure reduces pulmonary blood flow improving dyspnea
options.rationale: Right heart failure typically worsens exercise capacity and causes systemic congestion; it would be correct only in a scenario where reduced pulmonary flow paradoxically relieved pulmonary edema.

options.text: Enhanced peripheral vasodilation increases venous return and relieves symptoms
options.rationale: Peripheral vasodilation may transiently increase venous return but generally does not relieve symptoms of fixed outflow obstruction; this would be correct only with compensatory hemodynamic changes.

question: Which murmur description from the lecture best fits aortic stenosis on auscultation?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: A systolic crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border
options.rationale: Aortic stenosis produces a systolic ejection murmur that crescendos then decrescendos and is best heard at the right second intercostal space, as stated in the lecture.

options.text: A holosystolic murmur loudest at the cardiac apex
options.rationale: A holosystolic apical murmur indicates mitral regurgitation, not AS; it would be correct only if MR were present.

options.text: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border
options.rationale: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border is typical of AR, not AS; it would be correct only with aortic insufficiency.

options.text: A mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex
options.rationale: A mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap is characteristic of mitral stenosis, not AS; it would be correct only with MS.

options.text: A continuous machinery murmur heard throughout systole and diastole
options.rationale: A continuous machinery murmur suggests PDA and is unrelated to AS; it would be correct only if a PDA were the lesion.

question: Which of the following best explains why an S3 is more likely heard in mitral regurgitation with ventricular dilation?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Rapid filling of a dilated ventricle produces low frequency vibrations after S2
options.rationale: S3 arises from rapid early diastolic filling into an enlarged, compliant ventricle producing low-frequency sounds shortly after S2; MR with volume overload predisposes to S3 as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle produces a late diastolic sound
options.rationale: Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle produces S4 before S1, not S3; this would be correct only in pressure overload states with stiff ventricles.

options.text: Closure of the mitral valve produces a high pitched early systolic sound
options.rationale: Mitral closure produces S1 at systole onset and is high-pitched; S3 is low-pitched and diastolic, so this would be correct only if S1 were misidentified.

options.text: Delayed pulmonary valve closure causes a split second heart sound
options.rationale: Delayed pulmonary closure causes wide S2 splitting, unrelated to S3 generation; this would be correct only with right heart conduction delay.

options.text: A continuous flow lesion produces a machinery sound throughout the cycle
options.rationale: Continuous machinery murmurs (PDA) are not S3 and do not explain low-frequency diastolic gallops; this would be correct only with a PDA.

question: A patient with chronic aortic regurgitation is most likely to have which change in left ventricular systolic pressure compared with normal?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume, and associated electrical events and heart sounds that occur during a normal cardiac cycle.

options.text: Increased systolic pressure due to larger stroke volume from volume overload
options.rationale: Chronic AR increases LVEDV and stroke volume, which raises LV systolic pressure and often aortic systolic pressure, consistent with the lecture's description of AR hemodynamics.

options.text: Decreased systolic pressure due to impaired contractility
options.rationale: Decreased systolic pressure occurs with systolic dysfunction, not typically in compensated chronic AR where systolic pressure often rises; this would be correct only with decompensated LV failure.

options.text: Unchanged systolic pressure with markedly reduced diastolic pressure
options.rationale: AR usually increases systolic pressure while lowering diastolic pressure; unchanged systolic pressure would be correct only if compensatory mechanisms exactly balanced changes.

options.text: Markedly reduced systolic pressure with narrow pulse pressure
options.rationale: Narrow pulse pressure and low systolic pressure are not features of chronic AR and would be correct only in low output states without regurgitation.

options.text: Systolic pressure fluctuating widely beat to beat without pattern
options.rationale: Beat-to-beat fluctuation suggests arrhythmia or measurement artifact, not the predictable hemodynamic pattern of AR; this would be correct only with arrhythmia.

question: Which clinical vignette best tests understanding of the 'y' descent on the atrial pressure tracing?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: A tracing shows a rapid fall in atrial pressure immediately after the v wave when the AV valve opens
options.rationale: The 'y' descent reflects rapid atrial emptying into the ventricle after AV valve opening and follows the v wave, matching the lecture's description of atrial waveform components.

options.text: A tracing shows a pressure rise during atrial contraction before ventricular systole
options.rationale: A pressure rise during atrial contraction corresponds to the 'a' wave, not the 'y' descent; this would be correct only if the question targeted atrial systole.

options.text: A tracing shows a sustained plateau during ventricular ejection
options.rationale: A sustained plateau is not a named atrial waveform and does not describe the y descent; it would be correct only with atypical tracing morphology.

options.text: A tracing shows a bulge in atrial pressure during isovolumic contraction
options.rationale: A bulge during isovolumic contraction is the 'c' wave from valve bulging, not the y descent; this would be correct only if valve bulging were the focus.

options.text: A tracing shows a tall wave during ventricular systole from venous return
options.rationale: A tall wave during ventricular systole is the 'v' wave from venous filling, not the y descent; this would be correct only if the v wave were being described.

question: Which of the following best describes the effect of chronic mitral regurgitation on left ventricular end diastolic volume and why?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Increased LVEDV due to augmented filling from regurgitant volume returning each systole
options.rationale: MR causes systolic backflow into the LA which returns to the LV during diastole, increasing LVEDV and predisposing to volume overload and dilation, as explained in the lecture.

options.text: Decreased LVEDV due to impaired mitral inflow from valve narrowing
options.rationale: Decreased LVEDV occurs in mitral stenosis where inflow is impeded; MR increases LVEDV, so this would be correct only with MS rather than MR.

options.text: Unchanged LVEDV with isolated rise in LV systolic pressure
options.rationale: Isolated rise in LV systolic pressure without volume change is more typical of pressure overload (AS); MR alters volumes, so this would be correct only in pure pressure overload.

options.text: Transient LVEDV reduction during atrial systole only
options.rationale: Atrial systole transiently augments LV filling but does not reduce LVEDV chronically; this would be correct only in a very specific timing scenario.

options.text: Marked LVEDV fluctuation with each beat but no net change
options.rationale: MR produces a net chronic increase in LVEDV due to regurgitant volume accumulation, not mere beat-to-beat fluctuation; this would be correct only with perfect compensation.

question: A patient with severe aortic stenosis has a systolic murmur that peaks later in systole as severity increases. Which explanation from the lecture accounts for this change in murmur timing?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Prolonged left ventricular ejection time delays the murmur peak toward late systole
options.rationale: Severe AS prolongs LV ejection time as the ventricle works against higher resistance, shifting the systolic ejection murmur peak later in systole, consistent with lecture material.

options.text: Earlier closure of the mitral valve advances the murmur into early systole
options.rationale: Mitral closure timing affects S1 but does not shift the ejection murmur peak; murmur timing relates to ejection dynamics, so this would be correct only with altered mitral timing affecting ejection onset.

options.text: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance causing delayed P2
options.rationale: Delayed P2 affects S2 splitting, not the timing of a systolic ejection murmur from the aortic valve; this would be correct only if pulmonary events altered systolic ejection timing indirectly.

options.text: Sudden increase in stroke volume moving the murmur earlier
options.rationale: Increased stroke volume tends to make ejection murmurs peak earlier and louder; a later peak with severity is due to prolonged ejection, so this would be correct only in opposite physiology.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation causing variable murmur timing unrelated to valve severity
options.rationale: AF causes beat-to-beat variability but does not systematically shift murmur peak later with increasing AS severity; this would be correct only if rhythm variability dominated timing.

question: Which of the following best matches the lecture definition of cardiac output?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: The product of stroke volume and heart rate expressed in liters per minute
options.rationale: Cardiac output equals SV × HR (L/min), as explicitly defined in the lecture slides.

options.text: The difference between end diastolic and end systolic pressures
options.rationale: Pressure differences are not cardiac output; CO is a volume per time, so this would be correct only if pressure were converted to flow via resistance measurements.

options.text: The sum of left and right ventricular stroke volumes per beat
options.rationale: CO is per minute and typically refers to one ventricle's output; summing stroke volumes per beat is not the standard definition and would be correct only if clarified per minute.

options.text: The percentage of end diastolic volume ejected each beat
options.rationale: That describes ejection fraction, not cardiac output; this would be correct only if the question asked about EF.

options.text: The volume remaining in the ventricle after systole
options.rationale: Volume remaining after systole is end systolic volume, not cardiac output; this would be correct only if ESV were the target metric.

question: Which exam finding from the lecture would most strongly suggest chronic aortic regurgitation rather than acute regurgitation?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Left ventricular enlargement with a high amplitude systolic impulse
options.rationale: Chronic AR leads to LV dilation and increased stroke volume producing a forceful systolic impulse; acute AR lacks time for remodeling, so this finding favors chronic disease per the lecture.

options.text: Sudden hypotension with soft peripheral pulses
options.rationale: Sudden hypotension and weak pulses are features of acute severe AR due to lack of compensation; this would be correct only in acute presentations.

options.text: A loud early diastolic murmur without LV enlargement
options.rationale: A loud diastolic murmur can occur in both acute and chronic AR; LV enlargement distinguishes chronicity, so this would be correct only if chronic remodeling were absent.

options.text: Elevated jugular venous pressure with peripheral edema only
options.rationale: JVP elevation and peripheral edema reflect right heart failure and are not specific for chronic AR; this would be correct only with right heart involvement.

options.text: A mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap at the apex
options.rationale: A mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap indicates mitral stenosis, not AR; this would be correct only with MS.

question: Which of the following best explains why mitral stenosis produces a diastolic rumble rather than a systolic murmur?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Obstruction to flow occurs during ventricular filling when the mitral valve should be open
options.rationale: MS impedes blood flow from LA to LV during diastole (ventricular filling), producing a diastolic rumble and opening snap, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Valve leaflets fail to close during systole causing backflow
options.rationale: Failure to close during systole causes regurgitation and a systolic murmur (MR), not a diastolic rumble; this would be correct only with MR.

options.text: Semilunar valve obstruction during ejection produces diastolic sounds
options.rationale: Semilunar valve obstruction affects systolic ejection and produces systolic murmurs (AS), not diastolic rumble; this would be correct only with misassigned timing.

options.text: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle produces late systolic sound
options.rationale: Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle produces S4 before S1, not a diastolic rumble; this would be correct only in pressure overload states.

options.text: Continuous flow through a patent ductus produces a rumbling quality
options.rationale: A PDA produces a continuous machinery murmur, not a diastolic rumble at the apex; this would be correct only with a PDA.

question: Which hemodynamic measurement from the lecture would be increased in mitral stenosis compared with normal?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume and associated heart sounds/murmurs during specific phases of an abnormal cardiac cycle under the following conditions: aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Left atrial pressure due to impeded flow into the left ventricle
options.rationale: MS increases resistance to LV filling, raising LA pressure and causing pulmonary venous hypertension, as emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Left ventricular end diastolic volume due to increased preload
options.rationale: MS reduces LVEDV because inflow is impeded; increased LVEDV occurs in regurgitant lesions, so this would be correct only in MR or AR.

options.text: Aortic systolic pressure due to increased forward stroke volume
options.rationale: Aortic systolic pressure rises with increased stroke volume as in AR, not MS; this would be correct only with compensatory increased output.

options.text: Pulmonary arterial oxygen content due to improved gas exchange
options.rationale: MS typically worsens pulmonary congestion and gas exchange; increased pulmonary arterial oxygen content would be correct only with improved pulmonary function.

options.text: Right atrial pressure due to isolated left sided valve disease
options.rationale: Right atrial pressure may rise secondarily with long-standing MS causing right heart strain, but the primary and most direct increase is LA pressure; this would be correct only in advanced disease.

question: A 60-year-old with chronic aortic regurgitation is noted to have a high stroke volume and a diastolic murmur. Which compensatory mechanism described in the lecture explains the increased stroke volume?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the changes in aortic pressure, left ventricular pressure, left atrial pressure, left ventricular volume, and associated electrical events and heart sounds that occur during a normal cardiac cycle.

options.text: Frank-Starling mechanism increasing contractile force with higher preload
options.rationale: Increased LVEDV in AR augments sarcomere stretch and contractility via the Frank-Starling mechanism, raising stroke volume as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Baroreceptor mediated decrease in heart rate increasing stroke volume
options.rationale: Baroreceptor reflexes adjust HR but do not directly increase stroke volume via preload; the primary mechanism for increased SV in AR is Frank-Starling, so this would be correct only with specific reflex dominance.

options.text: Increased afterload causing greater ejection fraction
options.rationale: Increased afterload typically reduces ejection fraction; AR increases preload rather than afterload to raise SV, so this would be correct only in pressure overload states.

options.text: Enhanced atrial contraction producing larger atrial kick
options.rationale: Atrial kick contributes modestly to LV filling but is not the main driver of increased SV in chronic AR; this would be correct only if atrial contribution were disproportionately large.

options.text: Peripheral vasoconstriction increasing venous return transiently
options.rationale: Peripheral vasoconstriction can alter preload transiently but chronic increased SV in AR is due to volume overload and Frank-Starling effects; this would be correct only transiently.

question: Which of the following best represents the lecture's description of the isovolumic relaxation phase?
cited_learning_objective: Trace and label the individual parameters on the cardiac cycle Diagram (Wiggers diagram).

options.text: Ventricular pressure falls with both aortic and mitral valves closed
options.rationale: Isovolumic relaxation occurs after aortic valve closure with both semilunar and AV valves closed, causing falling ventricular pressure without volume change, as stated in the lecture.

options.text: Ventricular pressure rises with both valves closed during contraction
options.rationale: Rising pressure with closed valves describes isovolumic contraction, not relaxation; this would be correct only if the phase were contraction.

options.text: Rapid ventricular filling with open mitral valve
options.rationale: Rapid filling follows mitral opening and is not isovolumic; this would be correct only in diastole after relaxation completes.

options.text: Atrial contraction producing the a wave
options.rationale: Atrial contraction occurs later in diastole and produces the 'a' wave, not during isovolumic relaxation; this would be correct only with timing confusion.

options.text: Ejection of blood into the aorta with falling ventricular volume
options.rationale: Ejection occurs during systole with falling ventricular volume and rising aortic pressure; this is not isovolumic relaxation and would be correct only if ejection were misidentified.

question: A 70-year-old with long-standing hypertension develops an S4 gallop. Which ventricular property described in the lecture most directly produces S4?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the physiological and pathophysiological basis of normal and abnormal hearts sounds, respectively.

options.text: Decreased ventricular compliance causing atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
options.rationale: S4 results from atrial contraction into a noncompliant, stiff ventricle (e.g., hypertrophy from hypertension), producing a late diastolic low-frequency sound as explained in the lecture.

options.text: Rapid early diastolic filling of a dilated ventricle
options.rationale: Rapid filling into a dilated ventricle produces S3, not S4; this would be correct only in volume overload with dilation.

options.text: Closure of the semilunar valves at the end of systole
options.rationale: Semilunar valve closure produces S2, not S4; this would be correct only if the sound were S2.

options.text: Holosystolic regurgitant flow from the mitral valve
options.rationale: Holosystolic MR produces a pansystolic murmur, not S4; S4 is diastolic and due to atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so this would be correct only with MR.

options.text: A continuous murmur from a patent ductus arteriosus
options.rationale: A PDA causes a continuous machinery murmur unrelated to S4 generation; this would be correct only with a PDA present.
